title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 844–846 (Night 189, continuing nights-188), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 189 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. The vizier runs from the tower to King Shahramān and tells him that his son has lost his mind. The king, darkening, swears that if harm or madness has come to the boy through the vizier's counsel he will nail him to the dome, and goes with him to the tower. Qamar al-Zamān rises, kisses his father's hands, stands before him with bowed head, and asks forgiveness in verse. The king embraces him and tests his wits: the prince names the days of the week and the Arab months in order, and the king, delighted, spits in the vizier's face. Asked about the girl he claims slept beside him, Qamar al-Zamān laughs, says he can bear no more mockery, and declares he consents to marry — but only that girl, whom he is sure his father sent and then took away before morning. The king calls on God's protection over his son's wits, and dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ التَّاسِعَةُ وَالثَّمَانُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-tāsiʿatu wa-al-thamānūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the ninth and-the-eighty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and eighty-ninth night,
sentences.n: al-tāsiʿa, “the ninth”, agrees with al-layla, and the tens, al-thamānūna, follow in the same nominative case. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْوَزِيرَ خَرَجَ مِنَ الْبُرْجِ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ يَجْرِي إِلَى أَنْ دَخَلَ عَلَى الْمَلِكِ شَهْرَمَانَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-wazīra kharaja mina al-burji wa-lam yazal yajrī ilā an dakhala ʿalā al-maliki Shahramāna
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-vizier went-out from the-tower, and-not he-ceased running until that he-entered upon the-King Shahramān.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the vizier went out of the tower and ran on without stopping until he came in to King Shahramān.
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the story with the words that ended the last night. The print runs السعيد and ان together, السعيدان; read al-saʿīdu anna, and the spacing is kept. lam yazal with an imperfect, “he kept on”, and ilā an with a perfect, “until”. dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to (a person)”. Shahramāna, like other names in -ān, takes no tanwīn and has -a for the genitive.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلَ إِلَيْهِ قَالَ لَهُ الْمَلِكُ أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ مَا الَّذِي دَهَاكَ وَمَنِ الَّذِي بِشَرِّةِ رَمَاكَ وَمَالِي أَرَاكَ فِي ارْتِبَاكٍ حَتَّى جِئْتَ مَرْعُوبًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣala ilayhi qāla lahu al-maliku ayyuhā al-wazīru mā alladhī dahāka wa-mani alladhī bi-sharrihi ramāka wa-mā lī arāka fī irtibākin ḥattā jiʾta marʿūban
sentences.l: And-when he-arrived to-him, said to-him the-king: O vizier, what (is) that-which has-befallen-you, and-who (is) the-one-who with-his-evil has-struck-you, and-what (is) to-me (that) I-see-you in confusion, until you-have-come terrified?
sentences.i: When he reached him, the king said to him, “Vizier, what calamity has befallen you? Who has struck you with his malice? Why do I see you in such a flurry, that you come to me in terror?”
sentences.n: The king speaks in rhymed prose: dahāka, ramāka, arāka, irtibāk. dahā, “to befall”, is said of a calamity. The print writes بشرّة, with ة for the pronoun ه, as it does now and then; the shadda and the kasra under the ة are printed: read bi-sharrihi, “with his evil”. ramā bi-, “to strike (someone) with”: bi- marks what is thrown. The print runs ما and لي together, ومالي; the spacing is kept. mā lī arāka, “what is it with me that I see you”, that is, “why do I see you”. irtibāk, Form VIII verbal noun, “confusion, being in a tangle”. ḥattā with a perfect, “so much so that”. marʿūban, “terrified”, a clause of state in the accusative. The ئ of جئت is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ إِنِّي قَدْ جِئْتُكَ بِبِشَارَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu ayyuhā al-maliku innī qad jiʾtuka bi-bishāratin
sentences.l: So-he-said to-him: O king, indeed-I have come-to-you with-tidings.
sentences.i: He said to him, “O king, I have come to you with tidings.”
sentences.n: jāʾa bi-, “to bring”: the verb takes what is brought with bi-, as atā bi- does. bishāra is properly “good news”, and also the reward its bearer may claim; the vizier uses the word, as court speech does, of news he dreads to give, and the king will throw it back at him. The ئ of جئتك is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْمَلِكُ وَمَا هِيَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-maliku wa-mā hiya
sentences.l: So-said to-him the-king: And-what (is) she?
sentences.i: The king said to him, “And what are they?”
sentences.n: hiya, “she, it”, takes up the feminine bishāra.

sentences.t: قَالَ لَهُ اعْلَمْ أَنَّ وَلَدَكَ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ ذَهَبَ عَقْلُهُ وَحَصَلَ لَهُ جُنُونٌ
sentences.tr: qāla lahu iʿlam anna waladaka Qamara al-Zamāni dhahaba ʿaqluhu wa-ḥaṣala lahu junūnun
sentences.l: He-said to-him: Know that your-son Qamar al-Zamān, has-gone his-mind, and-has-come-about to-him madness.
sentences.i: He said to him, “Know that your son Qamar al-Zamān has lost his mind, and madness has come upon him.”
sentences.n: iʿlam, “know”, the imperative that opens a weighty statement. anna waladaka … dhahaba ʿaqluhu: the son is the noun of anna, and the clause after it tells what befell him, “his mind has gone”. ḥaṣala li-, “to come about for, befall”: li- marks the one it befalls.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْمَلِكُ كَلَامَ الْوَزِيرِ صَارَ الضِّيَاءُ فِى وَجْهِهِ ظَلَامًا وَقَالَ لَهُ أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ أَوْضِحْ لِي صِفَةَ جُنُونِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-maliku kalāma al-wazīri ṣāra al-ḍiyāʾu fī wajhihi ẓalāman wa-qāla lahu ayyuhā al-wazīru awḍiḥ lī ṣifata junūnihi
sentences.l: And-when heard the-king (the) words (of) the-vizier, became the-light in his-face darkness, and-he-said to-him: O vizier, make-clear to-me (the) description (of) his-madness.
sentences.i: When the king heard what the vizier said, the light in his face turned to darkness, and he said to him, “Vizier, tell me plainly what form his madness takes.”
sentences.n: ṣāra, “to become”, takes its predicate in the accusative, ẓalāman. ḍiyāʾ, “light, brightness”; its ء is printed, and so is the ى of فى. awḍiḥ, imperative of Form IV awḍaḥa, “to make clear”. ṣifa, “description, manner”.

sentences.t: قَالَ لَهُ يَاسَيِّدِي سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً ثُمَّ أَعْلَمَهُ أَنَّهُ قَدْ جَرَى مِنْهُ كَذَا وَكَذَا وَأَخْبَرَةُ بِمَا تَمَّ لَهُ مَعَهُ
sentences.tr: qāla lahu yā sayyidī samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan thumma aʿlamahu annahu qad jarā minhu kadhā wa-kadhā wa-akhbarahu bi-mā tamma lahu maʿahu
sentences.l: He-said to-him: O-my-master, hearing and-obedience. Then he-informed-him that-it had happened from-him thus and-thus, and-he-told-him with-what had-come-to-pass to-him with-him.
sentences.i: “My master,” he said to him, “with hearing and obedience.” Then he told him that the prince had done this and that, and told him all that had befallen him at the prince's hands.
sentences.n: The print runs يا and سيّدي together, ياسيّدي, with its shadda printed; the spacing is kept. samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan, “with hearing and obedience”, accusatives standing for a verb left unsaid. aʿlama, Form IV, “to inform”: here aʿlamahu annahu, “he informed him that”, the -hu of annahu being the pronoun of the matter, “that the fact was”. jarā min, “to issue from, be done by”. kadhā wa-kadhā, “such and such”: the narrator does not repeat what the reader already knows. The print writes واخبرة, with ة for the pronoun ه: read wa-akhbarahu, “and he told him”. akhbara bi-, “to tell of”: bi- marks the thing told, here mā, “what”. tamma lahu maʿahu, “had come to pass for him with him”: the first -hu is the vizier, the second the prince. The shadda of تمّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْمَلِكُ أَبْشْرْ أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ فَإِنِّي أُعْطِيكَ فِي نَظِيرِ بِشَارَتِكَ إِيَّايَ بِجُنُونِ وَلَدِي ضَرْبَ رَقَبَتِكَ وَزَوَالَ النِّعْمَةِ عَنْكَ يَا أَنْحَسَ الْوُزَرَاءِ وَأَنْجَسَ الْأُمَرَاءِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-maliku abshir ayyuhā al-wazīru fa-innī uʿṭīka fī naẓīri bishāratika iyyāya bi-junūni waladī ḍarba raqabatika wa-zawāla al-niʿmati ʿanka yā anḥasa al-wuzarāʾi wa-anjasa al-umarāʾi
sentences.l: So-said to-him the-king: Rejoice, O vizier! For-indeed-I give-you, in return-for your-bringing-good-news (to) me of (the) madness (of) my-son, (the) striking (of) your-neck and-(the)-passing (of) the-favour from-you, O most-ill-omened (of) the-viziers and-most-unclean (of) the-emirs!
sentences.i: The king said to him, “Rejoice, vizier! For in return for your glad tidings of my son's madness I will reward you with the striking off of your head and the loss of every favour, you most ill-starred of viziers, foulest of emirs!
sentences.n: The king turns the vizier's word bishāra against him: the bearer of good news looks for a reward, and this is the reward he will have. abshir, imperative of Form IV abshara, “rejoice, take the good news”, is bitter irony. The print sets a sukūn on the shīn of ابشْر, where the imperative abshir has a kasra; the printed mark is kept where it stands, and the word is read abshir. fī naẓīri, “in return for”. bishāratika iyyāya, “your bringing me good news”: the verbal noun keeps a verb's object, and since its own suffix -ka is taken by the doer, the object is carried by the free pronoun iyyā-; the shadda of ايّاي is printed. bi-junūni waladī: bi- marks what the news was of. ḍarb al-raqaba, “striking of the neck”, is beheading. The insults rhyme, al-wuzarāʾ, al-umarāʾ: anḥas, “most ill-omened”, and anjas, “most unclean”, are elatives annexed to the group they top, in the accusative after yā.

sentences.t: لِأَنِّي أَعْلَمُ أَنَّكَ سَبَبُ جُنُونِ وَلَدِي بِمَشُورَتِكَ وَرَأْيِكَ الْفَاسِدِ التَّعِيسِ الَّذِي أَشَرْتَ بِهِ عَلَيَّ فِى الْأَوَّلِ وَالْآخِرِ
sentences.tr: li-annī aʿlamu annaka sababu junūni waladī bi-mashūratika wa-raʾyika al-fāsidi al-taʿīsi alladhī asharta bihi ʿalayya fī al-awwali wa-al-ākhiri
sentences.l: Because-I know that-you (are the) cause (of the) madness (of) my-son, by-your-counsel and-your-opinion, the-corrupt, the-wretched, which you-pointed with-it upon-me in the-first and-the-last.
sentences.i: For I know that you are the cause of my son's madness, with your counsel and the rotten, wretched advice you pressed on me from first to last.
sentences.n: li-annī, “because I”: li- of the reason with anna. sabab, “cause”, the predicate of anna, annexed to what it causes. bi-mashūratika, “by your counsel”: bi- of the means. taʿīs, “wretched, ill-fated”. ashāra ʿalā bi-, Form IV, “to advise (someone) to (something)”: ʿalā marks the one advised and bi- the advice, here the -hi taking up raʾy. fī al-awwali wa-al-ākhiri, “in the first and the last”, from beginning to end. The hamza of رأيك, the shadda of عليّ, the ى of فى and the madda of الآخر are printed.

sentences.t: وَاللَّهِ إِنْ كَانَ يَأْتِي عَلَى وَلَدِي شَيْءٌ مِنَ الضَّرَرِ أَوِ الْجُنُونِ لَأَسْمُرَّنَّكَ عَلَى الْقُبَّةِ وَأُذِيقُكَ النَّكْبَةَ
sentences.tr: wa-Allāhi in kāna yaʾtī ʿalā waladī shayʾun mina al-ḍarari awi al-junūni la-asmurannaka ʿalā al-qubbati wa-udhīquka al-nakbata
sentences.l: And-by-God, if it-is (that) comes upon my-son a-thing of the-harm or the-madness, I-will-surely-nail-you on the-dome, and-I-make-you-taste the-calamity!
sentences.i: By God, if any harm or madness should come upon my son, I will nail you up on the dome and make you taste disaster!”
sentences.n: wa-Allāhi, “by God”: the wāw of the oath. in kāna yaʾtī, “if it should be that there comes”, kāna with an imperfect in the condition. la-asmurannaka, “I will surely nail you”: the lām that answers an oath, with the energetic ending -anna. samara, “to nail”, which Lane gives beside the commoner Form II sammara. The print sets the shadda of لاسمرّنك on the rā, where the energetic wants it on the nūn; the printed mark is kept where it stands, and the word is read la-asmurannaka. It may instead be the shadda of Form II, la-usammirannaka, set one letter off; the sense is the same. wa-udhīquka, Form IV adhāqa, “to make taste”, goes on in the plain imperfect, where Classical Arabic would keep the energetic, wa-la-udhīqannaka. The king rhymes: al-qubba, al-nakba. awi takes a helping -i before the joining alif; the ء of شيء is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَ نَهَضَ قَائِمًا عَلَى أَقْدَامِهِ وَأَتَى بِهِ إِلَى الْبُرْجِ وَدَخَلَ فِيهِ عَلَى قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malika nahaḍa qāʾiman ʿalā aqdāmihi wa-atā bihi ilā al-burji wa-dakhala fīhi ʿalā Qamari al-Zamāni
sentences.l: Then indeed the-king rose, standing on his-feet, and-came with-him to the-tower, and-entered in-it upon Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: Then the king rose to his feet, brought the vizier with him to the tower, and went in to Qamar al-Zamān there.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then”, the narrator's way of opening a new move. nahaḍa qāʾiman ʿalā aqdāmihi, “he rose up, standing on his feet”, a full-length way of saying he got up at once; qāʾiman is a clause of state, and its ئ is printed. aqdām, plural of qadam, “foot”, is used of one man's two feet, as often. atā bi-, “to bring”: the verb chooses bi-; the -hi is the vizier. dakhala fīhi ʿalā, “he went into it, in to (him)”: fī the place, ʿalā the person.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلَا إِلَيْهِ وَثَبَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ عَلَى الْأَقْدَامِ وَنَزَلَ سَرِيعًا مِنْ فَوْقِ السَّرِيرِ الَّذِي هُوَ جَالِسٌ عَلَيْهِ وَقَبَّلَ يَدَيْ وَالِدِةِ وَتَأَخَّرَ وَرَاءَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣalā ilayhi wathaba Qamaru al-Zamāni ʿalā al-aqdāmi wa-nazala sarīʿan min fawqi al-sarīri alladhī huwa jālisun ʿalayhi wa-qabbala yaday wālidihi wa-taʾakhkhara warāʾahu
sentences.l: And-when the-two-arrived to-him, leapt Qamar al-Zamān onto the-feet, and-came-down quickly from on-top-of the-couch which he (was) sitting on-it, and-kissed (the) two-hands (of) his-father, and-drew-back behind-him.
sentences.i: When the two of them reached him, Qamar al-Zamān sprang to his feet and came quickly down from the couch where he was sitting, kissed his father's hands, and stepped back.
sentences.n: waṣalā, the dual, “the two of them arrived”, the king and the vizier. wathaba ʿalā al-aqdām, “he leapt onto his feet”. alladhī huwa jālisun ʿalayhi, “which he was sitting on”: the -hi of ʿalayhi takes up the couch, as an Arabic relative clause requires. yaday, “the two hands of”, the dual in annexation, which drops its -ni. The print writes والدة and وراءة, with ة for the pronoun ه: read wālidihi, “his father”, and warāʾahu, “behind him”, that is, backwards. taʾakhkhara, Form V, “to draw back”: he does not presume to stand close to his father. The hamza of وتأخر and the ء of وراءة are printed.

sentences.t: وَأَطْرَقَ بِرَأْسِهِ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ وَهُوَ مُكَتَّفُ الْيَدَيْنِ إِلَى وَرَائِهِ قُدَّامَ أَبِيهِ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ كَذٰلِكَ سَاعَةً زَمَانِيَّةً
sentences.tr: wa-aṭraqa bi-raʾsihi ilā al-arḍi wa-huwa mukattafu al-yadayni ilā warāʾihi quddāma abīhi wa-lam yazal kadhālika sāʿatan zamāniyyatan
sentences.l: And-he-bowed with-his-head to the-ground, and-he (was) bound (of) the-two-hands to his-back, before his-father; and-not he-ceased thus an-hour of-time.
sentences.i: He bowed his head to the ground and stood before his father with his hands clasped behind his back, and so he stayed for a good while.
sentences.n: aṭraqa, Form IV, “to bow the head, look down”, in silence or shame; bi-raʾsihi, “with his head”: bi- marks the part bowed. wa-huwa mukattafu al-yadayni, “he being pinioned of the hands”, a clause of state: mukattaf is the passive participle of Form II kattafa, “to pinion”, said here of a man who holds his arms behind him in humility before his lord; it is annexed to al-yadayn, “the two hands”, to say in what part he is so. quddāma, “in front of”. sāʿatan zamāniyyatan, “a while of time”, the stock phrase for “a good while”. The hamzas of برأسه and ورائه are printed.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ رَفَعَ رَأْسَهُ إِلَى وَالِدِةِ وَفَرَّتِ الدُّمُوعُ مِنْ عَيْنَيْهِ وَسَالَتْ عَلَى خَدَّيْهِ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika rafaʿa raʾsahu ilā wālidihi wa-farrati al-dumūʿu min ʿaynayhi wa-sālat ʿalā khaddayhi wa-anshada yaqūlu
sentences.l: And-after that he-raised his-head to his-father, and-sprang the-tears from his-two-eyes and-flowed on his-two-cheeks, and-he-recited, saying:
sentences.i: After that he raised his head to his father, and the tears sprang from his eyes and ran down his cheeks, and he recited:
sentences.n: Again والدة, with ة for the pronoun ه: read wālidihi. farrat, “they sprang, broke away”, from farra, “to flee”; it takes a helping -i before the joining alif. The ḍamma of الدموعُ, the hamza of رأسه and the shadda of خدّيه are printed. ʿaynayhi, khaddayhi, duals, “his two eyes, his two cheeks”. anshada yaqūlu, “he recited, saying”, the stock words that bring in a poem.

sentences.t:
اِنْ كُنْتُ قَدْ اَذْنَبْتُ ذَنْبًا سَالِفًا * فِيْ حَقِّكُمْ وَاَتَيْتُ شَيْأً مُنْكَرًا
اَنَا تَائِبٌ عَمَّا جَنَيْتُ وَعَفْوُكُمْ * يَسَعُ الْمُسِيءَ اِذَا اَتَى مُسْتَغْفِرًا
sentences.tr:
in kuntu qad adhnabtu dhanban sālifan * fī ḥaqqikum wa-ataytu shayʾan munkarā
anā tāʾibun ʿammā janaytu wa-ʿafwukum * yasaʿu al-musīʾa idhā atā mustaghfirā
sentences.l:
If I-have already sinned a-sin past * in your-due, and-brought a-thing disapproved,
I (am) repenting of-what I-committed; and-your-pardon * is-wide-enough-for the-wrongdoer when he-comes seeking-forgiveness.
sentences.i:
If I have sinned against you in time past, and done a thing that should not be done,
I repent of the wrong I did; and your pardon is wide enough for any offender who comes asking forgiveness.
sentences.n: Metre: kāmil, rhyming in -rā. The pointing is the print's own: it writes the hamza as a bare vowel on the alif (اِنْ, اَذْنَبْتُ, اَنَا), and the sukūn on the yā of فِيْ marks the long vowel. adhnaba dhanban, “to sin a sin”, the cognate accusative. fī ḥaqqikum, “with regard to you, against what is your due”: the plural -kum is respect for his father. atā shayʾan munkaran, “to do a thing disapproved”; munkar is what law and decency reject. Line 2: the answer to in, “if”, stands without the fa- prose would want, as verse allows. tāʾib ʿan, “repenting of”. janā, “to commit (a wrong)”. yasaʿu, imperfect of wasiʿa, “to be wide enough for, hold”. al-musīʾ, “the wrongdoer”, active participle of Form IV asāʾa. mustaghfir, Form X participle, “asking forgiveness”, a clause of state after atā. At the rhyme, -an is read -ā.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ قَامَ الْمَلِكُ وَعَانَقَ وَلَدَهُ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ وَقَبَّلَهُ بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهِ وَأَجْلَسَهُ إِلَى جَانِبِهِ فَوْقَ السَّرِيرِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika qāma al-maliku wa-ʿānaqa waladahu Qamara al-Zamāni wa-qabbalahu bayna ʿaynayhi wa-ajlasahu ilā jānibihi fawqa al-sarīri
sentences.l: So-at that, rose the-king and-embraced his-son Qamar al-Zamān, and-kissed-him between his-two-eyes, and-seated-him at his-side on-top-of the-couch.
sentences.i: At that the king rose, embraced his son Qamar al-Zamān and kissed him between the eyes, and sat him down beside him on the couch.
sentences.n: fa-ʿinda dhālika, “thereupon”. ʿānaqa, Form III, “to embrace”. qabbalahu bayna ʿaynayhi, “he kissed him between his eyes”, on the brow, a father's kiss; the shadda of وقبّله is printed. ajlasa, Form IV, “to seat”. ilā jānibihi, “at his side”: with a verb of placing, ilā marks where a thing comes to rest.

sentences.t: وَالْتَفَتَ إِلَى الْوَزِيرِ وَنَظَرَ إِلَيْهِ بِعَيْنِ الْغَضَبِ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا كَلْبَ الْوُزَرَاءِ كَيْفَ تَقُولُ عَلَى وَلَدِي قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ مَا هُوَ كَذَا وَكَذَا وَتَرْعَبُ قَلْبِي عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-iltafata ilā al-wazīri wa-naẓara ilayhi bi-ʿayni al-ghaḍabi wa-qāla lahu yā kalba al-wuzarāʾi kayfa taqūlu ʿalā waladī Qamari al-Zamāni mā huwa kadhā wa-kadhā wa-tarʿabu qalbī ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And-he-turned to the-vizier, and-looked at-him with-(the)-eye (of) the-anger, and-said to-him: O dog (of) the-viziers, how (do) you-say against my-son Qamar al-Zamān what is thus and-thus, and-you-terrify my-heart for-him?
sentences.i: Then he turned to the vizier, looked at him with an angry eye, and said to him, “You dog of a vizier, how can you say such things of my son Qamar al-Zamān, and fill my heart with fear for him?”
sentences.n: The print has العضب, a misprint for الغضب, corrected here: bi-ʿayni al-ghaḍabi, “with the eye of anger”, the stock phrase for an angry look; bi- of the manner. iltafata ilā, Form VIII, “to turn towards”. kalb al-wuzarāʾ, “dog of the viziers”, the worst of them. qāla ʿalā, “to say against, say of (someone, to his harm)”. mā huwa kadhā wa-kadhā, “what is such and such”: the king will not repeat it. raʿaba, Form I, “to frighten”, with ʿalā of the one feared for.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ الْتَفَتَ الْمَلِكُ إِلَى وَلَدِهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا وَلَدِي مَا اسْمُ هٰذَا الْيَوْمِ
sentences.tr: thumma iltafata al-maliku ilā waladihi wa-qāla lahu yā waladī mā ismu hādhā al-yawmi
sentences.l: Then turned the-king to his-son and-said to-him: O my-son, what (is the) name (of) this the-day?
sentences.i: Then the king turned to his son and said to him, “My son, what day is this?”
sentences.n: The king tests his son's wits with the plainest questions he can think of. mā ismu, “what is the name of”: ism begins with a joining alif, so no hamza is written, and mā ismu is said mā-smu.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ يَا وَالِدِي هٰذَا يَوْمُ السَّبْتِ وَغَدًا يَوْمُ الْأَحَدِ وَبَعْدَهُ يَوْمُ الِاثْنَيْنِ وَبَعْدَهُ الثُّلٰثَاءُ وَبَعْدَهُ الْأَرْبِعَاءُ وَبَعْدَهُ الْخَمِيسُ وَبَعْدَهُ الْجُمُعَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu yā wālidī hādhā yawmu al-sabti wa-ghadan yawmu al-aḥadi wa-baʿdahu yawmu al-ithnayni wa-baʿdahu al-thulāthāʾu wa-baʿdahu al-arbiʿāʾu wa-baʿdahu al-khamīsu wa-baʿdahu al-jumuʿatu
sentences.l: So-he-said to-him: O my-father, this (is the) day (of) the-Sabbath, and-tomorrow (the) day (of) the-first, and-after-it (the) day (of) the-two, and-after-it the-third, and-after-it the-fourth, and-after-it the-fifth, and-after-it the-gathering.
sentences.i: He said to him, “Father, today is Saturday, and tomorrow is Sunday, and after it Monday, then Tuesday, then Wednesday, then Thursday, then Friday.”
sentences.n: The days are counted from Sunday, al-aḥad, “the first”: al-ithnayn, “the two”, and al-thulāthāʾ, al-arbiʿāʾ and al-khamīs from the numbers three, four and five. Saturday is al-sabt, “the Sabbath”, and Friday al-jumuʿa, “the gathering”, for the congregational prayer. The print spells الثلثاء without the long ā, as it spells ثلثة; the dagger alif supplies it, al-thulāthāʾ. al-ithnayni, genitive dual after yawm, begins with a joining alif. ghadan, “tomorrow”, an adverb in the accusative, here heads its clause: “and tomorrow is”. wa-baʿdahu, “and after it”: the -hu takes up each day in turn.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْمَلِكُ يَا وَلَدِي يَا قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ عَلَى سَلَامَةِ عَقْلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-maliku yā waladī yā Qamara al-Zamāni al-ḥamdu li-llāhi ʿalā salāmati ʿaqlika
sentences.l: So-said to-him the-king: O my-son, O Qamar al-Zamān, the-praise (be) to-God for (the) soundness (of) your-mind!
sentences.i: The king said to him, “My son, Qamar al-Zamān, praise be to God that your mind is sound!
sentences.n: yā Qamara al-Zamāni: a name that is an annexation is called in the accusative. al-ḥamdu li-llāhi ʿalā, “praise be to God for”: li- marks the one praised, ʿalā the thing he is praised for. salāma, “soundness, safety”.

sentences.t: مَا اسْمُ هٰذَا الشَّهْرِ الَّذِي عَلَيْنَا بِالْعَرَبِيِّ
sentences.tr: mā ismu hādhā al-shahri alladhī ʿalaynā bi-al-ʿarabiyyi
sentences.l: What (is the) name (of) this the-month which (is) upon-us, in-the-Arabic?
sentences.i: What is the name of this month we are in, in Arabic?”
sentences.n: alladhī ʿalaynā, “which is upon us”, the month now running. bi-al-ʿarabiyyi, “in Arabic”: bi- names the language. The prince answers with the months of the Muslim lunar year.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ اسْمُهُ ذُوالْقَعْدَةِ وَيَلِيهِ ذُوالْحِجَّةِ وَبَعْدَهُ الْمُحَرَّمُ وَبَعْدَهُ صَفَرٌ وَبَعْدَهُ شَهْرُ رَبِيعٍ الْأَوَّلِ وَبَعْدَهُ شَهْرُ رَبِيعٍ الْآخِرِ وَبَعْدَهُ جُمَادَي الْأُولَى وَبَعْدَهُ جُمَادَي الْأُخْرَى وَبَعْدَهُ رَجَبٌ وَبَعْدَهُ شَعْبَانُ وَبَعْدَهُ رَمَضَانُ وَبَعْدَهُ شَوَّالٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ismuhu dhū al-qaʿdati wa-yalīhi dhū al-ḥijjati wa-baʿdahu al-muḥarramu wa-baʿdahu ṣafarun wa-baʿdahu shahru rabīʿin al-awwali wa-baʿdahu shahru rabīʿin al-ākhiri wa-baʿdahu jumādā al-ūlā wa-baʿdahu jumādā al-ukhrā wa-baʿdahu rajabun wa-baʿdahu shaʿbānu wa-baʿdahu ramaḍānu wa-baʿdahu shawwālun
sentences.l: So-he-said: Its-name (is) Dhū al-Qaʿda, and-follows-it Dhū al-Ḥijja, and-after-it al-Muḥarram, and-after-it Ṣafar, and-after-it (the) month (of) Rabīʿ the-First, and-after-it (the) month (of) Rabīʿ the-Last, and-after-it Jumādā the-First, and-after-it Jumādā the-Other, and-after-it Rajab, and-after-it Shaʿbān, and-after-it Ramaḍān, and-after-it Shawwāl.
sentences.i: He said, “It is Dhū al-Qaʿda, and after it comes Dhū al-Ḥijja, then al-Muḥarram, then Ṣafar, then the month of Rabīʿ the First, then the month of Rabīʿ the Second, then Jumādā the First, then Jumādā the Second, then Rajab, then Shaʿbān, then Ramaḍān, then Shawwāl.”
sentences.n: The prince runs through the twelve lunar months from the present one round to the month before it. The print runs ذو and القعدة, and ذو and الحجة, together; the spacing is kept: dhū al-qaʿda, “the one of sitting”, and dhū al-ḥijja, “the one of the pilgrimage”. yalīhi, “follows it”, from waliya. The print writes جمادي with a dotted ي for the final ى: read Jumādā. Ṣafar, Rajab and Shawwāl take tanwīn; Shaʿbān and Ramaḍān, with their -ān ending, do not. al-ukhrā, “the other”, feminine of ākhar, stands where the usual name is Jumādā al-ākhira. The shadda of المحرّم and the madda of الآخر are printed.

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَ بِذٰلِكَ الْمَلِكُ فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا وَبَصَقَ فِي وَجْهِ الْوَزِيرِ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا شَيْخَ السُّوءِ كَيْفَ تَزْعُمُ أَنَّ وَلَدِي قَدْجُنَّ وَالْحَالُ أَنَّهُ مَاجُنَّ إِلَّا أَنْتَ
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥa bi-dhālika al-maliku faraḥan shadīdan wa-baṣaqa fī wajhi al-wazīri wa-qāla lahu yā shaykha al-sūʾi kayfa tazʿumu anna waladī qad junna wa-al-ḥālu annahu mā junna illā anta
sentences.l: So-rejoiced at-that the-king a-rejoicing great, and-he-spat in (the) face (of) the-vizier, and-said to-him: O old-man (of) the-evil, how (do) you-claim that my-son has gone-mad, and-the-state (is) that-it: not went-mad except you?
sentences.i: The king was overjoyed at this. He spat in the vizier's face and said to him, “You wicked old man, how dare you claim that my son has gone mad, when no one here has gone mad but you?”
sentences.n: fariḥa bi-, “to rejoice at”: bi- marks the cause; faraḥan shadīdan, the cognate accusative of degree. baṣaqa, “to spit”. shaykh al-sūʾ, “old man of evil”, a wicked old man; the ء of السوء is printed. zaʿama anna, “to claim (falsely) that”. junna, passive of janna, “he was possessed”, that is, “he went mad”: the jinn have taken him. The print runs قد and جنّ, and ما and جنّ, together, with their shaddas printed; the spacing is kept. wa-al-ḥālu annahu, “while the case is that”, a later way of saying “whereas in fact”; the -hu of annahu is the pronoun of the matter. mā … illā anta, “none … but you”.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ حَرَّكَ الْوَزِيرُ بِرَأْسِهِ وَأَرَادَأَنْ يَتَكَلَّمَ ثُمَّ خَطَرَ بِبَالِهِ أَنْ يَتَمَهَّلَ قَلِيلًا لِيَنْظُرَ مَا ذَا يَكُونُ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika ḥarraka al-wazīru bi-raʾsihi wa-arāda an yatakallama thumma khaṭara bi-bālihi an yatamahhala qalīlan li-yanẓura mā dhā yakūnu
sentences.l: So-at that, moved the-vizier with-his-head, and-wanted that he-speak; then it-occurred in-his-mind that he-wait a-little, so-that-he-see what that will-be.
sentences.i: At that the vizier shook his head and was about to speak; then it crossed his mind to hold back a little and see what would come of it.
sentences.n: ḥarraka bi-raʾsihi, “he moved his head”, shook it: bi- marks the part set moving, as with aṭraqa bi-raʾsihi above; the shadda of حرّك and the hamza of برأسه are printed. The print runs اراد and ان together, وارادان; the spacing is kept: wa-arāda an, “and he wanted to”. khaṭara bi-bālihi, “it passed through his mind”: bi- of the place the thought passes; bāl, “mind”. tamahhala, Form V, “to take one's time”; its shadda is printed. li-yanẓura, “so that he might see”: li- of purpose with the subjunctive. mā dhā, “what”, printed as two words.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَ قَالَ لِوَلَدِهِ يَا وَلَدِي أَيُّ شَيْءٍ هٰذَا الْكَلَامُ الَّذِي تَكَلَّمْتَ بِهِ لِلْخَادِمِ وَالْوَزِيرِ حَيْثُ قُلْتَ لَهُمَا إِنِّي كُنْتُ نَائِمًا مَعَ صَبِيَّةٍ مَلِيحَةٍ فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malika qāla li-waladihi yā waladī ayyu shayʾin hādhā al-kalāmu alladhī takallamta bihi li-al-khādimi wa-al-wazīri ḥaythu qulta lahumā innī kuntu nāʾiman maʿa ṣabiyyatin malīḥatin fī hādhihi al-laylati
sentences.l: Then indeed the-king said to-his-son: O my-son, what thing (is) this the-talk which you-spoke with-it to-the-servant and-the-vizier, where you-said to-the-two: Indeed-I was sleeping with a-girl lovely in this the-night?
sentences.i: Then the king said to his son, “My son, what is this talk you have been giving the servant and the vizier, telling them that you slept with a lovely girl this night?
sentences.n: li-waladihi, “to his son”: li- marks the one spoken to. ayyu shayʾin, “what thing?”, the later way of asking “what?”; the shadda of ايّ and the ء of شيء are printed. takallama bi-, Form V, “to speak (words)”: bi- marks what is said, the -hi taking up al-kalām; li-al-khādimi marks the hearers, where Classical Arabic says takallama maʿa. ḥaythu, “where”, here “in that, when”, a later usage. qulta lahumā innī, “you said to the two of them, ‘I …’”: after qāla the words reported take inna. nāʾiman, the predicate of kuntu, in the accusative; its ئ and the shaddas of تكلّمت and صبيّة are printed.

sentences.t: فَمَا شَأْنُ هٰذِهِ الصَّبِيَّةِ الَّتِي ذَكَرْتَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-mā shaʾnu hādhihi al-ṣabiyyati allatī dhakartahā
sentences.l: So-what (is the) affair (of) this the-girl whom you-mentioned-her?
sentences.i: What is the story of this girl you spoke of?”
sentences.n: shaʾn, “affair, business”: mā shaʾnu, “what is the matter of”. The print writes شان without its hamza, as it mostly leaves hamza out. dhakartahā, “you mentioned her”: the -hā takes up allatī, as a relative clause requires. The shadda of الصبيّة is printed.

sentences.t: فَضَحِكَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ مِنْ كَلَامِ أَبِيهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا أَبِي اعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ مَا بَقِيَ لِي قُوَّةٌ تَتَحَمَّلُ السُّخْرِيَّةَ فَلَا تَزِيدُوا عَلَيَّ شَيْأً وَلَا بِكَلِمَةٍ وَاحِدَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaḥika Qamaru al-Zamāni min kalāmi abīhi wa-qāla lahu yā abī iʿlam annahu mā baqiya lī quwwatun tataḥammalu al-sukhriyyata fa-lā tazīdū ʿalayya shayʾan wa-lā bi-kalimatin wāḥidatin
sentences.l: So-laughed Qamar al-Zamān from (the) words (of) his-father, and-said to-him: O my-father, know that-it: not remained to-me strength (that) bears the-mockery; so-not add (pl.) upon-me a-thing, and-not with-a-word single.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān laughed at his father's words and said to him, “Father, know that I have no strength left to bear mockery; so do not add a thing more to it, not one single word.
sentences.n: ḍaḥika min, “to laugh at”: min gives the cause. annahu, the pronoun of the matter again. mā baqiya lī quwwatun, “there remains to me no strength”: the verb stays masculine before its feminine subject, as often, and li- marks the owner. tataḥammalu, Form V, “that can bear”, an indefinite relative clause with no relative word. sukhriyya, “mockery”. lā tazīdū, “do not add”, the jussive plural: he speaks to his father and those about him together. zāda ʿalā, “to add to (someone's load)”. wa-lā bi-kalimatin wāḥidatin, “and not with a single word”: bi- of the means, “not by so much as a word”. The print spells شيأ with its hamza on the alif, and prints the shadda of عليّ.

sentences.t: فَقَدْ ضَاقَ خُلْقِي مِمَّا تَفْعَلُونَهُ مَعِي
sentences.tr: fa-qad ḍāqa khulqī mimmā tafʿalūnahu maʿī
sentences.l: For-indeed has-become-narrow my-temper from-what you (pl.) do-it with-me.
sentences.i: My patience is worn thin by what you are all doing to me.
sentences.n: ḍāqa khulqī, “my temper has grown narrow”, the later idiom for being at the end of one's patience; khulq, “character, temper”. mimmā, min + mā, “from what”: min gives the cause. faʿala maʿa, “to do to”, as in the last night; the -hu of tafʿalūnahu takes up mā.

sentences.t: وَاعْلَمْ يَا أَبِي عِلْمًا يَقِينًا أَنِّي قَدْ رَضِيتُ بِالزَّوَاجِ وَلٰكِنْ بِشَرْطِ أَنْ تُزَوِّجَنِى تِلْكَ الصَّبِيَّةَ الَّتِى كَانَتْ نَائِمَةً عِنْدِي فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-iʿlam yā abī ʿilman yaqīnan annī qad raḍītu bi-al-zawāji wa-lākin bi-sharṭi an tuzawwijanī tilka al-ṣabiyyata allatī kānat nāʾimatan ʿindī fī hādhihi al-laylati
sentences.l: And-know, O my-father, a-knowing certain, that-I have consented to-the-marriage; but on-(the)-condition that you-marry-me that the-girl who was sleeping with-me in this the-night.
sentences.i: And know for certain, Father, that I have consented to marry, but on condition that you marry me to that girl who was sleeping beside me this night.
sentences.n: ʿilman yaqīnan, “a certain knowledge”, the cognate accusative after iʿlam: “know for certain”. raḍiya bi-, “to consent to”: bi- marks what is accepted, as in the last night. bi-sharṭi an, “on condition that”: bi- of the terms. zawwaja, Form II, “to marry (a man to a woman)”, here with two plain objects, the man and the bride, where in the last night, with tazawwaja, “to marry”, the bride came after bi-; its shadda is printed. The print writes the final ي of تزوّجنى and of التى as ى, as it often does. wa-lākin, “but”, is spelled as always without its long ā, which the dagger alif supplies. nāʾimatan, the predicate of kānat; its ئ is printed.

sentences.t: فَإِنِّي أَتَحَقَّقُ أَنَّكَ أَنْتَ الَّذِي أَرْسَلْتَهَا إِلَيَّ وَشَوَّفْتَنِى إِلَيْهَا وَبَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ أَرْسَلْتَ إِلَيْهَا قَبْلَ الصُّبْحِ وَأَخَذْتَهَا مِنْ عِنْدِي
sentences.tr: fa-innī ataḥaqqaqu annaka anta alladhī arsaltahā ilayya wa-shawwaftanī ilayhā wa-baʿda dhālika arsalta ilayhā qabla al-ṣubḥi wa-akhadhtahā min ʿindī
sentences.l: For-indeed-I am-certain that-you, you (are) the-one-who sent-her to-me and-made-me-look (?) to-her; and-after that you-sent to-her before the-dawn, and-took-her from with-me.
sentences.i: For I am sure that it was you who sent her to me and set me longing for her, and then, before dawn, sent for her and took her away from me.”
sentences.n: taḥaqqaqa, Form V, “to be sure of”. annaka anta alladhī arsaltahā, “that you are the one who sent her”: after a head in the first or second person, the verb of the relative clause may take that person, arsalta, “you sent”, rather than arsala. The print's وشوّفتنى, with its shadda and the fatḥa on its tāʾ printed, is doubtful. As it stands it is shawwafa, Form II of shāfa, “to see”, the later word for “to show”, “to make (someone) see”: “you made me look to her”, which sits awkwardly with ilayhā. With one dot more, شوّقتنى, shawwaqtanī ilayhā, “you made me long for her”, gives just the sense wanted, and the compositor may have dropped it; but the print can be read as it stands, so it is kept and vocalised so, and the idiomatic line follows the likelier sense. The final ى stands for ي, as often. arsala ilā, “to send to”: he sent someone to her, to fetch her. min ʿindī, “from beside me”. The shadda of اليّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ اسْمُ اللَّهِ حَوَالَيْكَ يَا وَالِدِي سَلَامَةُ عَقْلِكَ مِنَ الْجُنُونِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-maliku ismu Allāhi ḥawālayka yā wālidī salāmatu ʿaqlika mina al-junūni
sentences.l: So-said the-king: (The) name (of) God (be) around-you, O my-father! (The) safety (of) your-mind from the-madness!
sentences.i: The king said, “God's name be about you, my child! May your mind be kept safe from madness!”
sentences.n: ismu Allāhi ḥawālayka, “the name of God be round about you”, the formula the vizier used in the last night, to ward off harm from one who seems possessed; the fatḥa on the lām of حوالَيك is printed. yā wālidī, “O my father”, said by the father to his son: a parent may call a child by the name the child calls him, a turn of tenderness Arabic still uses. salāmatu ʿaqlika mina al-junūni, “safety of your mind from madness”, a wish in the nominative, with its predicate left unsaid. A moment ago the king thanked God for his son's sound mind; now the girl is back in the talk.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night.
